script.title: In 1939, three US states had two Thanksgivings
sentences: In 1939, three American states got two Thanksgivings.
That November had five Thursdays, and the last one fell on November 30.
Stores feared that left too few shopping days before Christmas.
So President Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving up a week, to November 23.
Football teams had already scheduled their rivalry games for the old date.
The mayor of Atlantic City started calling it Franksgiving.
Twenty-three states took the new date, and twenty-two kept the old one.
Colorado, Mississippi and Texas simply gave holidays in both weeks.
A 1941 survey found the extra shopping week hadn't really boosted sales.
script.description:
In 1939 Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving a week early to add Christmas shopping days.
Half the states refused, and three took both days off.
claims_en: In 1939 Colorado, Mississippi and Texas gave holidays in both weeks, i.e. on both Thanksgiving dates.
In 1939 November had five Thursdays and the last one fell on November 30.
There was concern that this left too few shopping days before Christmas; business leaders feared lost sales.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving one week earlier, to November 23, 1939.
Many college football teams had scheduled rivalry games for the last day in November.
The term Franksgiving was coined by Charles D. White, the mayor of Atlantic City, in 1939.
Twenty-three states and DC recognized the new date and twenty-two states kept November 30.
A 1941 Commerce Department survey found no significant expansion of retail sales due to the change.
